senses: The sawdust-like byproduct of wood-boring insects like woodworm, termites, old-house borers or powderpost beetles.
ety: Borrowed from German Fraß.
examples: Examine the stalk, especially behind the sheaths, for holes and sawdustlike frass where the larvae have entered to tunnel in the stalk.

senses: Nothing, zero.
ety: Probably from Joe Zilch, a placeholder name (compare John Doe) used by Nunnally Johnson in his column in the Brooklyn Daily Eagle from 1923; in turn from Joe Zilch, an unseen character referenced in comedian Frank Tinney's stage routine. Compare the rare German surname Zilch.
examples: Her search for decent home-made winter clothes came up with zilch, so she had to get imported stuff.

senses: Any soluble pigment used for dyeing the hair, fabric, etc.
ety: From dye + stuff.
examples: Except for the indigo, the dyebaths are steeped over heat to release their pigment and then strained to remove the dyestuff.

senses: To make worse (a problem, bad situation, negative feeling, etc.).
ety: First attested in 1660; borrowed from Latin exacerbātus, perfect passive participle of Latin exacerbō (“to provoke”) (see -ate (verb-forming suffix)), from ex- (“out of; thoroughly”) + acerbō (“to embitter, harshen or worsen”).
examples: The proposed shutdown would exacerbate unemployment problems.

senses: Intoxicated by alcohol.
Inclined to consume a significant amount of alcohol.
Involving a large consumption of alcohol.
Containing or cooked with alcohol.
ety: From booze + -y.
examples: We all had hangovers after a boozy weekend in town.
Once the concert was over I settled back into my boozy routine, wine at home with my family, cognac in my studio when I was composing.
For dessert, the hosts treated us to a helping of boozy apple pie.

senses: Radiating from a center; having rays or parts diverging from a center; radiated.
Surrounded by rays, such as the head of a saint in a religious picture; (heraldry) radiant.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin radiātus (see Etymology 1 and -ate (adjective-forming suffix) for more).
examples: On a wreath of the colors argent and tenné four lightning flashes barbed radiate pilewise of the first, a Roman helm or garnished gules.

senses: A self-evident or obvious truth.
A banality or cliché.
ety: From true + -ism.
examples: It is a truism that the site of stations is conditioned by history and geography, but Dover Marine especially owes its fascinating and unusual layout to these two factors.
It is a truism that the people who attend a rally for President Trump more than two years before he’s on the ballot again are generally strong supporters of President Trump.
The phrase If something exists, there is porn of it used to be a clever internet meme; now it’s a truism.

senses: Synonym of fusil, a light musket or firelock.
ety: From French fusil, ultimately from Late Latin focus (“fire”).
examples: He had not been many days at the chateau, when he perceived, with surprize and consternation, that his steps were continually watched by two servants armed with fusees.

senses: Anything transmitted by word of mouth, such as a fable, legend, narrative, story, or tale (especially a poetic tale).
A story or set of stories relevant to or having a significant truth or meaning for a particular culture, religion, society, or other group; a myth, a mythology.
A set of assumptions or beliefs about something.
A recurring theme; a motif.
ety: Borrowed from Late Latin mȳthos (“myth”), from Ancient Greek μῦθος (mûthos, “report, tale, story”). Doublet of myth. The plural form mythoi is from Ancient Greek μῦθοι (mûthoi), and the form mythoses from mythos + -es.
examples: In addition to mythoi drawn from myths and fairy tales, romances also employ mythoi derived from chivalric romances.

senses: A four-wheeled horse-drawn carriage with collapsible half-hood, two double seats facing each other, and an outside seat for the driver.
ety: From dialectal German Barutsche, from Italian baroccio, from Late Latin *birotium, from Latin birotus (“chariot”), from bi- (“two”) + rota (“wheel”). The spelling was altered in English as if the word had come from French. Doublet of britchka.
examples: Day was drooping on a fine evening in March as a brown barouche passed through the wrought-iron gates of Hare-Hatch House on to the open highway.

senses: A narrow board, usually thicker at one edge than the other, used as siding for houses and similar structures of frame construction.
Such boards, arranged horizontally and overlapping with thick edge down, collectively, as siding.
ety: From Middle English clapholt, partial translation from Middle Low German klappholt or Middle Dutch klapholt (“barrel stave”), from klappen (“to crack”) + holt (“wood”). The part "holt" was later calqued to "board".
examples: Its exterior is covered with clapboards stained dark brown.
Bond turned to the window and watched the pretty clapboard houses slip by as they approached Trenton. He loved trains and he looked forward with excitement to the rest of the journey.

senses: A low chest of drawers on short legs.
A stand for a washbowl and jug.
A chair containing a chamber pot.
A kind of woman's headdress, raising the hair and fore part of the cap to a great height.
ety: Borrowed from French commode (literally “convenient”). Doublet of comodo.
examples: Now under high Commodes with Looks Erect, Bare-fac’d devours in gawdy Colours deck.

senses: A mean (unkind or miserly) person; a killjoy.
ety: From mean + -ie.
examples: Teacher kept me in after school again. What a meanie!
That meanie wouldn't even lend me the bus fare.
The indigent health-care bill died in the waning moments of the session, killed by Republican Representative Bill Ceverha of Dallas, a notorious meanie.

senses: The state or condition of being blocked.
The thing that is the cause of such a state, blocking a passage.
ety: From block + -age.
examples: There was a blockage in the sewer, so we called out the plumber.

senses: Synonym of sarcastic.
ety: From sarc (“sarcasm”) + -y.
examples: Zilch at the bookshop. The little fat one wasn't backstage at all. The thin sarky one briefly, but he was with Colin Smy all the time.

Full of Coxon's trademark sarky lyricism, this 14-track concept album celebrates and laments the bittersweet nature of love, avoiding being dull or mawkish by being so gorgeous and satisfyingly coherent.
It would seem that during his Bournemouth team’s recent 2-1 defeat at Sheffield United, referee Jon Moss gave the hosts some “soft fouls” and made “little sarky comments” that “didn’t help”.

senses: A general uproar or commotion.
Violent anger or frenzy.
A state of intense excitement.
ety: From Middle English furour, from Middle French fureur, from Old French furor, from Latin furor, from furō (“To rage, to be out of one's mind”).
examples: This action created a furor in the broader medical community. It was considered undoctorly, unprofessional, illegal, and an infringement on the right to practice.
The verdict of not guilty created a true furor in the courtroom.
The story of the princess's affair caused a furor among journalists.

senses: The state of being lax; looseness, lack of tension.
Moral looseness; lack of rigorousness or strictness.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French laxité, itself borrowed from Latin laxitas, laxitatem, from laxus. By surface analysis, lax + -ity.
examples: It is no accident that capital punishment is reentering our society on the wave of the conservative reaction to the permissiveness and laxity of the past two decades.

senses: A type of small family-owned business — often a casual, usually outdoor restaurant (in both countries) or convenience store (in Indonesia).
ety: Borrowed from Malay warung.
examples: Daud Yusof who runs one of the four warungs in the kampung said his business has been affectred because of the flies and claimed his earnings from selling nasi berlauk has dropped by 40 percent.
Walking allows us to know precisely what kind and where to put convenient and comfort shelters like public toilets, benchs, kiosks, warungs and wakafs.

senses: Tawny-colored.
ety: Borrowed from Latin fulvus (“reddish-brown”).
examples: It was a minute anatomical and generally descriptive account of the large fulvous Ourang-Outang of the East Indian Islands.
The upper wings of the moth which Jacob held were undoubtedly marked with kidney-shaped spots of a fulvous hue.

senses: A Russian movement in modern art characterized by the creation of nonrepresentational geometric objects using industrial materials.
A style of modern architecture that flourished in the Soviet Union in the 1920s and early 1930s.
A psychological epistemology which argues that humans generate knowledge and meaning from their experiences.
A school of studying international relations that prioritises the way the behaviour of polities and agents in geopolitics is constructed by norms and identities.
ety: From constructive + -ism.
examples: Constructivism wasn't just Russian state propaganda - its blend of optimism and pragmatism and its emphasis on equality and the collective prefigured key developments in 20th-century art.
Art in the first half of the 20th century was powerfully shaped by Constructivism and Supremicism in the East and by Cubism, Futurism, and Surrealism in the West.
Many masterpieces of Soviet constructivism are now crumbling under capitalism, replaced by pastiche architecture or pale replicas of former buildings.

senses: A covered pouch, usually one of a pair, laid across the back of a horse, donkey, or mule behind its saddle, or hanging over the rear wheel of a motorcycle; often made of leather or (on a motorcycle) a rigid material.
Loose fatty flesh on a person's upper thighs or buttocks, that hangs like saddlebags.
A style of house with two rooms separated by a small hall and open space.
ety: From saddle + bag.
examples: There was no camp, bedroll, or fire and no other sign of a man, just the saddled horse with saddlebags and packs tied on behind it.
The area treated was always the side of the thighs, where she had visible saddlebags.

senses: A member of the Spanish nobility, especially one without a title.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish hidalgo. Doublet of fidalgo.
examples: The young man seems to entertain but an imperfect appreciation of the respect due from a menial to a Castilian hidalgo.

senses: To cancel funding for.
ety: From de- + fund.
examples: Did the Arizona legislators satisfy the principles of deliberation when they decided to defund organ transplants?
However, when Congress has attempted to defund a presidential agency, presidents have responded by creating new agencies to perform similar functions.

senses: A collection of hadith arranged according to the Companion who transmitted them from Muhammad.
ety: Arabic مُسْنَد (musnad), passive participle of أَسْنَدَ (ʔasnada, “support, evidence”).
examples: Mahmud al-Khwarazmi (593/ 1197-655/1257), a well-travelled Hanafite scholar who ended his career as a teacher in Baghdad, composed a kind of super-musnad of Abu Hanifa.

In these cases, the musnad was a scholarly exercise undertaken by some later admirer who would cull all of the hadīth a particular figure quotes in his works and elsewhere and place them in a single book.
The type of hadīṯ collection called musnad is one in which compilers brought together reports whose chains of transmission go back to a particular Companion of the Prophet.

senses: A composition adapted to sacred words in the elaborate polyphonic church style; an anthem.
ety: From French motet.
examples: Singing their holiday concert from memory, the group sounded confident and expressive in pieces ranging from a medley of Barry Manilow songs to renaissance motets.

senses: A shoemaker or cobbler.
ety: Inherited from Middle English soutere, from Old English sūtere, from Latin sūtor (“shoemaker, cobbler”).
examples: There is no work better than another to please God : to pour water , to wash dishes , to be a souter (cobbler) , or an apostle

senses: Having been cut or stabbed with a knife.
Wearing or carrying (a specified type of) knife (utensil or tool).
Having a knife (blade-like part) of the specified type.
ety: From knife + -ed.
examples: The police were on the pavement outside; the knifed man lay holding his side with blood through his fingers spreading up his cheap shirt like litmus paper turning red.
It is despicable what the sharp-knifed general and his army have done to the honorable Commander Francisco Caso y Luengo, one of our most revered Spanish military figures.
A short-knifed wheat header, such as is used in harvesting wheat and barley in California, if especially strongly built, has been suggested as a practicable contrivance.

senses: A hand gesture used to depict the meaning of a song
ety: Borrowed from Sanskrit हस्त (hasta).
examples: A prudent prayer, and a vigorous dance, with many interwoven leaps and twirls and pirouettes, and hastas all around.

senses: Characterized by anticipation.
ety: From anticipate + -ory.
examples: The children were all wearing anticipatory grins as the cake was served.

senses: Redundant use of words, a pleonasm, an unnecessary and tedious repetition.
An expression that features tautology.
ety: From Late Latin tautologia, from Ancient Greek ταὐτολογία (tautología) from ταὐτός (tautós, “the same”) + λόγος (lógos, “explanation”). By surface analysis, tauto- + -logy.
examples: It is tautology to say, "Forward Planning".
The expression "raze to the ground" is a tautology, since the word "raze" includes the notion "to the ground".
Pure mathematics consists of tautologies, analogous to ‘men are men’, but usually more complicated.

senses: The study of handwriting, especially as a means of analyzing a person's character.
A system of handwriting.
ety: From French graphologie, coined by Jean-Hippolyte Michon from Ancient Greek γραφή (graphḗ, “writing”) + French -logie (“study of”). By surface analysis, grapho- + -logy.
examples: Near-synonym: psychographology (sometimes synonymous)
The philosopher Ludwig Klages saw graphology as a means to penetrate the deceptive self-presentation of his contemporaries and unveil their true character.
Graphology and graphological deviation are likely to be very significant in a mode that lacks non-textual social cues, such as paralanguage, prosody and gesture.

senses: A male who has been castrated, especially a male whose testicles have been removed before puberty in order to retain his boyish voice.
A male soprano or alto voice produced by castration of the treble singer before puberty, intended to conserve his voice; the singer.
ety: From Italian castrato, from Latin castrō (“to castrate”), likely from caedō (“to cut”).
examples: A castrato stepped forward, a slender / young man with earnest grey eyes.
As contexts shift, so does generational taste. Just ask the castrati – the high-voiced boy singers displaced when Enlightenment liberalism restored female performers to the stage.

senses: The emotional imprint of a trauma such as grief, loss, or degradation.
ety: From Middle French eschare (now escarre) or Late Latin eschara (“scar, scab”), from Ancient Greek ἐσχάρα (eskhára, “hearth, brazier, scab”). Doublet of scar.
examples: In another minute there was no letter; but, as with every other relationship in my life, an eschar of ashes. The word is rare, but exact.

senses: To apply rosin to (something); to rub or cover with rosin.
ety: From Old French raisine, rousine, variants of résine. Doublet of resin.
examples: We waited expectantly as the guest violinist rosined his bow in preparation for playing.
The devil opened up his case and he said, "I'll start this show." And fire flew from his fingertips as he rosined up his bow.

senses: A style of Latin American popular music, originally developing from reggae in Panama but now more of a type of hip hop-dance music mainly associated with Puerto Rico.
ety: Borrowed from Spanish reggaeton.
examples: The Spanish islands gave the world salsa, and the more modern (and often controversial) hip-hop style reggaeton, which was forged between the islands and Miami.

senses: An area of around the size of a parking space, used for recreation or as scenery.
ety: From park + -let.
examples: The Bison system has been used for parklets in San Francisco and New York City.
District 11 Supervisor Ahsha Safai is proposing to waive new, initial curbside parklet permit fees and offer a rebate for businesses that may have already paid them.

senses: Someone who makes or sells cheese.
Someone who adds cheese to a pizza in an assembly line.
A cocktail sandwich made with cheese.
A small spool that is used in the finishing stage of yarn-making.
ety: From Middle English cheser; equivalent to cheese + -er. The smile is said to resemble the uniform white coloration of cheese, or possibly related to the phrase say cheese.
examples: With Swiss farmers, Swiss cheesers, Swiss merchants, the best of grasses and water, and intelligent management, it cannot fail to produce an article which has reduced importation of foreign cheese to a minimum.
We took off our long, white cheesers' coats and hung them on the knobs of Edam, which is a Dutch cheese made of cows' milk with about forty per cent fat content and bright red outside.
But Terry Voice was the best pizza cheeser I've ever seen.

senses: A passage of several notes sung to one syllable of text.
The use of such passages.
ety: From Ancient Greek μέλισμα (mélisma, “song”), from μελίζω (melízō, “(I) sing, modulate; (I) celebrate in song”), from μέλος (mélos, “song, tune, melody; limb, part; member”).
examples: A choir sang one of the Lamentations of Jeremiah. The mournful melisma accompanied the slow procession to the palace built by Herod the Great, at present untenanted.
At the top of the hill in the archway of the main house, an eyeless old man sat on a bucket, scratching at a two-stringed gourd, warbling weird melismas on a madman's text.
A subsequent generation of singers, including Ms. Aguilera, Jennifer Hudson and Beyoncé, built their careers around melisma.

senses: The development of a bishop by moving it one square to a long diagonal; specifically, a set of opening moves where a bishop is developed to the second rank of the adjacent knight file.
ety: From Italian fianchetto, diminutive of fianco (“flank”).
examples: I’m not a hero, I’m not even a chessboard knight. Trying to be a priest was something of a fianchetto wasn’t it? Clever move by a poor player.

senses: A double layer of cloth worn by women as a scarf, veil etc.
ety: Borrowed from Hindustani (Hindi दुपट्टा (dupaṭṭā) / Urdu دُوپَٹَّہ (dūpaṭṭa)).
examples: Her dupatta slipped from her shoulders, as he encircled her waist with one hand.
Red bangles are stacked all the way to her elbows and her glittering scarlet dupatta is pinned to the high mound of her hair.
